Description: Undocumented/unapproved AI tool deployments by internal teams.
Vulnerability risks from dependency libraries, or third-party tools (e.g., a compromised open-source package or a poisoned pre-trained model pulled from a public model hub).
Sensitive data exposed through third-party tools & API calls.
Data processed across risky jurisdictions.
Unsafe or misleading model outputs executed without proper validation.
Weaknesses in CI/CD or model deployment processes.

Vulnerabilities related to critical dependencies on third-party libraries or frameworks (e.g., an unpatched CVE in a core ML framework, or an outage/breaking change at a foundation-model API provider).
Decisions made without sufficient oversight or validation.
Malicious data injected during training to manipulate model behavior.
Attackers reconstruct or identify training data from model outputs.
No mechanisms to track model performance, bias, usage, or anomalies or absence of regular audit.
Feedback loops when model outputs influence future inputs.
Alert systems can fail to notify or can overwhelm operators.
Malicious or negligent actions by employees or contractors.

A type of attack in which an attacker deliberately alters input data to mislead the model (e.g., prompt injection to bypass safety filters, or imperceptible image perturbations that fool a vision classifier).
Performance degradation due to changing data distributions.
Skewed results due to biased training data or model design (implicit only).

Harmful side-effects the model produces without explicit intent or anticipation by its designers (e.g., blackmail-like manipulation to avoid shutdown, or circumvention of its own safety safeguards during testing, poor pipeline design without proper validation for the outcomes).
Model safety mechanisms interfere with valid outputs.
The data distribution differs from training or model is not suitable for the deployment context.
Inability to interpret or justify model decisions.
Unclear who is responsible for the failures.
In case of custom development and deployment, legal risks may arise.

Model outputs are intercepted or altered in transit/storage so a downstream system acts on a manipulated result while believing it’s genuine (e.g., a man-in-the-middle attack altering a fraud-score before it reaches a decision engine).
Confidential system prompts, internal instructions, or embedded credentials are extracted by end users via crafted queries, exposing business logic or guardrail design.

Weaknesses in embedding generation, storage, or retrieval (e.g., cross-tenant access to a shared vector database, embedding inversion revealing source documents, or poisoned documents injected into a retrieval corpus).

Uncontrolled or excessive inference requests degrade availability or generate runaway compute costs (e.g., oversized prompts or high-volume requests exhausting GPU capacity or inflating API billing), also known as Denial of Wallet/Service.
